A.explanation: Too small for a $240 \text{ N}$ weight acting about $1.6 \text{ m}$ away. It ignores the correct force and perpendicular distance combination.

B.explanation: This is $W \times 1.6 \times \sin 20^{\circ}$, using the wrong trigonometric component for the horizontal distance from the vertical weight.

C.explanation: Weight $\approx 235 \text{ N}$ times horizontal distance $1.6\cos 20^{\circ}$ gives about $350 \text{ N m}$.

D.explanation: This is $W \times 1.6$ with no $\cos 20^{\circ}$ factor, treating the tilted $1.6 \text{ m}$ beam as if it were horizontal.

hints: Notice the 24 kg child is $1.6 \text{ m}$ from the central pivot along the beam tilted at $20^{\circ}$ to the horizontal, with weight acting vertically down.
Recall moment equals force times perpendicular distance, so you need the horizontal distance from the pivot to the line of the weight.
Connect the $1.6 \text{ m}$ along the beam to its horizontal projection using $\cos 20^{\circ}$, then multiply by $W = mg$.
walkthrough: Weight of the 24 kg child acts vertically down: $W = mg = 24 \times 9.81 \approx 235 \text{ N}$.
Distance along the beam from centre pivot to child is half of $3.2 \text{ m}$, so $d = 1.6 \text{ m}$.
Because the beam is at $20^{\circ}$ to the horizontal and the force is vertical, the perpendicular moment arm is the horizontal distance: $d_{perp} = 1.6 \cos 20^{\circ}$.
Calculate: $235 \times 1.6 \approx 376$ and $376 \times 0.940 \approx 354 \text{ N m}$, about $350 \text{ N m}$ with sensible precision. This is option C.
